ai-at-work.title: Caterpillar is bringing to AI deployment what it learned from automating mining
ai-at-work.excerpt: Caterpillar has spent decades putting autonomous machines to work at remote mining sites. It's now bringing that experience to AI deployment.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Caterpillar is taking what it learned from deploying autonomous equipment in mines—managing complex systems in harsh, remote environments with minimal human intervention—and applying that playbook to rolling out AI across its operations. This matters because most companies are still treating AI deployment like a software update, not like the decades-long operational transformation it actually is. The real insight here is that Caterpillar figured out something others are slow to learn: you can't just flip a switch on transformative tech and hope your people catch up.

ai-at-work.title: Why the next wave of AI startups won’t optimize infrastructure – until they have to
ai-at-work.excerpt: For most AI startups, infrastructure isn’t the first problem to solve; speed is. At the earliest stages, success is defined by how quickly a team can move from idea to product, from prototype to tract
ai-at-work.dwp_take: AI startups are prioritizing speed to market over infrastructure optimization because they're burning through limited cash and need to prove their concept works before investors lose patience. Digital workplace pros need to understand this because it means the AI tools landing in your organizations will have technical debt baked in from day one, requiring eventual painful refactoring. Nothing says "enterprise solution" quite like bolting on infrastructure fixes after you've already convinced 500 companies to depend on your product.

ai-at-work.title: Four safeguards to stop your AI agents from going rogue
ai-at-work.excerpt: Artificial intelligence agents are moving from experimentation to production, and with this shift, the stakes are rising. A coding agent at PocketOS recently deleted an entire production database. An
ai-at-work.dwp_take: AI agents are going into production at scale, and they're already making expensive mistakes like deleting databases and exposing user data. Digital workplace pros need to understand these risks because AI agents are about to become standard tools in our environments, handling real work with real consequences. The irony is rich: we've spent three decades building governance frameworks for humans, and now we get to do it all over again for machines that don't even have the excuse of being tired on a Monday morning.

ai-at-work.title: Andreessen Horowitz raises $1.1B AI infrastructure fund for chips, robots and more
ai-at-work.excerpt: Andreessen Horowitz today announced that it has raised a $1.1 billion fund to back artificial intelligence infrastructure startups. The Machine Age Fund will invest in companies that make data center
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Andreessen Horowitz just dropped $1.1 billion into a fund betting on AI infrastructure startups, focusing on chips, data centers, and edge hardware. This matters because the real constraint on AI adoption in enterprise isn't the software anymore, it's the plumbing, and whoever controls that hardware layer controls the game. Meanwhile, most organizations are still struggling to get Teams adoption right, so watch how long before this trillion-dollar bet on infrastructure meets the actual reality of your company's network bottleneck and IT procurement process.

industry-news.title: A Startup Brought Back ‘Twitter’ — Now X Is Suing
industry-news.excerpt: Operation Bluebird has launched Twitter.now while fighting X over rights to the Twitter name, betting nostalgia and AI tools can build a new social network. The post A Startup Brought Back ‘Twitter’ —
industry-news.dwp_take: A startup called Operation Bluebird launched Twitter.now as a nostalgic alternative to X, and now Elon Musk's company is suing them over the Twitter name. This matters because it shows how platform fragmentation is creating real headaches for workplace comms teams trying to figure out where their communities actually live. Honestly, if your organization spent the last two years migrating away from Twitter only to see it come back as a scrappy startup challenger, you'd have every right to just order pizza and pretend work ended in 2019.

industry-news.title: ARIA Bans Fully AI-Generated Songs From Australian Music Charts
industry-news.excerpt: ARIA now requires Australian chart-eligible music to be substantially human-made, excluding songs where AI creates the primary creative elements. The post ARIA Bans Fully AI-Generated Songs From Austr
industry-news.dwp_take: The Australian Recording Industry Association has banned fully AI-generated music from their official charts, requiring that human artists create the primary creative elements. This matters because it signals how content governance bodies are drawing lines around what counts as "real" work in an AI-flooded world, a question your organization will face sooner or later. The irony is delicious: we spent decades automating human creativity out of existence, and now we're legally defining creativity back into the job description.

industry-news.title: Cyberattack on Three UK Airports Exposes Data of 8.7 Million Customers
industry-news.excerpt: A cyberattack on Manchester Airports Group exposed information belonging to about 8.7 million customers across three UK airports. The post Cyberattack on Three UK Airports Exposes Data of 8.7 Million
industry-news.dwp_take: Hackers breached Manchester Airports Group systems and grabbed personal data on 8.7 million customers across three major UK airports. This matters because it shows that even heavily regulated, security-conscious organizations handling millions of transactions are still vulnerable to attacks, which means your workplace security protocols probably need stress-testing too. The real kicker is that someone's holiday photos and passport details are now floating around the dark web because a critical infrastructure operator didn't lock their digital doors tight enough.

industry-news.title: How AI and automation empower MSPs
industry-news.excerpt: How intelligent automation helps MSPs deliver stronger, faster cyber resilience.
industry-news.dwp_take: Managed service providers are using AI and automation tools to detect threats faster and respond to security incidents with less manual intervention. This matters because digital workplace teams increasingly depend on MSPs to keep their infrastructure secure, and faster threat response directly reduces downtime and risk for end users. That said, I'd pump the brakes on the word "empower" here—what's really happening is MSPs are finally getting tools to do what they should have been doing all along, which is staying ahead of threats instead of playing catch-up.
